5: A thread-to-barb fitting connects a threaded port to flexible tubing.
6: A thread-to-barb fitting connects a threaded port to flexible tubing. One end screws into a pump, valve, manifold or mating fitting; the other enters the tubing, whose contact with the barb provides sealing and retention. Common terms include threaded hose barb fitting and threaded-to-barb adapter.
7: Specify thread, port sealing structure and tubing ID together. '1/4 to 3.2' is incomplete: 1/4 can refer to different thread standards, while 3.2 might mean tubing ID, OD or fitting bore.
8: FOREACH SA straight and SAL elbow fittings use thread sealing with PTFE tape or compatible thread sealant. SB straight, SBS short straight and SBR rotary straight fittings use bottom-face contact sealing without tape or sealant. SC has M6×1 or 1/4-28 UNF female threads, typically receiving a mating rigid-tube fitting. PP, PA, POM and PVDF availability depends on the complete model.
9: How do thread-to-barb fittings seal at the port and tubing ends?
10: SA/SAL use auxiliary material in the engaged threads to close leakage paths. SB/SBS/SBR use thread-generated axial force to press the bottom shoulder face against the mating port face. Their threads primarily retain the fitting; keep the actual bottom sealing face clean and protected.
11: At the tubing end, the wall stretches over the barb and conforms to it for sealing and retention. Check thread and sealing structure at the equipment end, and ID, material, insertion depth and retention at the tube end. Tightening alone does not address both.

13: Check the threaded port, internal passage and barb connection separately; tightening one end does not correct a defect at the other.

21: How do UNF, NPT, metric and G threads relate to the sealing method?
22: Distinguish parallel from tapered threads, then identify the product's sealing structure. 10-32 UNF, 1/4-28 UNF, M5×0.8, M6×1 and G1/8 are parallel, with constant nominal diameter along the axis. 1/8-27 NPT and 1/4-18 NPT are tapered. Thread form describes engagement; the SA/SB series structure identifies where sealing occurs.

50: What is the difference between SA thread sealing and SB bottom-face sealing?
51: SA/SAL seal in the thread engagement using PTFE tape or fluid-compatible sealant. Wrap in the thread direction and control quantity to keep debris or excess sealant out of the passage. Thread sealing does not mean all models are tapered: SA-U28 is parallel UNF, while SA-1/8NPT is tapered NPT.
52: SB/SBS/SBR seal at the bottom shoulder face. Thread tightening presses it axially against the mating port face. Both surfaces must be clean and contact correctly. Do not use tape or sealant, or try to compensate for excessive port depth, scratches or a mismatched bottom face with tape.

111: Port section: verify M6×1, usable thread length, depth and sealing area so the faces meet correctly; merely being able to screw it in is insufficient.
112: Tubing: record OD, material, hardness and tolerances for the 3.2 mm ID tube. The catalog gives a 4.5 mm crest and 2.4 mm bore for assembly and passage assessment respectively.
113: Fluid: assess both the wash fluid and subsequent cleaning agents against PP and the tubing at actual concentration, temperature and contact time.
114: Space: allow tool access and tube bend radius, avoiding side loading or contact with adjacent parts.
115: Assembly: keep SBS bottom shoulder and mating port face clean; use no tape or sealant. Establish tightening requirements for the model and port material, then insert and support the tubing.
116: Performance: test leakage at specified pressure, temperature and start/stop conditions, and verify target flow. Add vacuum sealing checks for suction service.

119: How are thread-to-barb fittings installed, and which sealing materials and tools are needed?
120: Check and clean: verify the complete model, port threads and sealing faces; remove debris and inspect the barb for burrs, scratches and cracks.
121: Seal by series: apply PTFE tape in the thread direction or compatible sealant to SA/SAL, controlling amount and location. Clean SB/SBS/SBR bottom sealing faces and use no tape or sealant.
122: Align before tightening: confirm smooth engagement, then follow model and port-material requirements. Stop and inspect abnormal resistance; do not force crossed threads.
123: Use suitable tools on the designated surfaces. Where torque control is required, choose an appropriate-range torque tool; do not grip the barb or tubing with pliers.
124: Prepare tubing: cut square, remove debris and push axially to the specified position. Avoid repeated rocking that enlarges the end.
125: Support and retest: support tubing, fit suitable clamps if needed, then check leakage, air ingress, retention and flow under full operating conditions.
126: The assembly note for this series' PP, PA and POM plastic threaded fittings gives 0.25–0.30 N·m (±0.05 N·m), excluding NPT. Do not extend it to PVDF, metal fittings or other structures; also check port material and model requirements. NPT follows its own procedure. Record tool range, setting, sealing material and leak-test conditions for production.
127: Stop and depressurize before removal. Reused tubing ends may be stretched, indented or cracked; inspect and replace or prepare them as required by maintenance. Do not mask an excessively tight fit with unapproved grease, solvents or heating.

152: Does 3.2 mm mean tubing ID or OD?
153: In these model tables it means mating tubing ID, not crest OD or bore. SA-U28-32D, for example, takes 3.2 mm ID tubing, with a 4.5 mm crest and 2.4 mm bore.
155: No. 1/4-28 UNF is parallel with 28 threads per inch; SA-1/4NPT uses 1/4-18 NPT, tapered with 18 threads per inch. Dimensions, pitch and form differ. The same sealing material cannot make them interchangeable.
156: Do all thread-to-barb fittings require PTFE tape?
157: No. FOREACH SA/SAL use PTFE tape or compatible thread sealant. SB/SBS/SBR seal by bottom-face contact without either. SC female receivers follow the requirements of the mating rigid-tube fitting and sealing components.
158: What is the main difference between SA and SB?
159: SA seals in the engaged threads with auxiliary material; SB seals at the bottom shoulder face, with threads providing compression. SA-U28-32D-PP-N and SB-U28-32-PP-N both have 1/4-28 UNF male threads for 3.2 mm ID tubing, but require different port and assembly arrangements.
160: Can SBR rotary fittings be used for continuous rotation?
161: The name alone is insufficient. Continuous rotation needs defined speed, pressure, temperature, life and sealing performance. This article describes SBR's rotary construction without qualifying it as a continuous-duty rotary union.
162: Does a leak-free threaded end mean the complete connection passes?
163: Also verify barb/tubing fit, flow and actual duty. Check vacuum air ingress on suction lines, and relevant start/stop, heating and external-load conditions. Both sealing locations and tubing retention require separate validation.
